data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's terms as a non-inductive, pragmatic decision rule based on verisimilitude (truth-likeness), not probability.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If 'verisimilitude' implicitly relies on an inductive assumption that nature is uniform.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the definition of 'severe test' secretly encodes probabilistic expectations about evidence.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If acting on a theory logically entails believing it is more probable to succeed.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Popper distinguishes between the logical probability of a theory (which remains zero or low for universal laws) and its corroboration (a report on past performance). The scientist prefers the better-corroborated theory not because it is more likely to be true in the future (induction), but because it has withstood the severest tests so far, making it the best candidate for containing high verisimilitude. This is a critical preference, not a probabilistic one; we choose the theory that has survived our best attempts to kill it, acknowledging it may still be false tomorrow.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
